sudan.content: مرصد حقوقي يتهم «الدعم السريع» بقتل مدنيين في غرب كردفان - سودان تربيون تخطى الى المحتوى من نحن اتصل بنا English السبت , 21 نوفمبر - 2026 سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية سياسة الأخبار تقصي الحقائق اقتصاد دولي اقاليم الرأي English سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية اختيار المحرر مرصد حقوقي يتهم «الدعم السريع» بقتل مدنيين في غرب كردفان اختيار المحرر مرصد حقوقي يتهم «الدعم السريع» بقتل مدنيين في غرب كردفان 21 نوفمبر 2026 في اختيار المحرر , الأخبار , الحرب بين الجيش السوداني والدعم السريع , كردفان 0 منازل مدنيين تحترق في بلدة أبو قلب بغرب كردفان عقب غارة جوية لطيران الجيش- الأحد 15 نوفمبر 2026 الأبيض 20 نوفمبر 2026 – اتهم مرصد حقوقي، السبت، قوات الدعم السريع بقتل ثلاثة مواطنين في منطقة “أبو قلب” بولاية غرب كردفان، فيما تحدث ناشطون عن عمليات قتل ذات طابع عرقي ترتكبها القوات ذاتها ضد المدنيين في البلدة. وخلال الأسبوع المنصرم، شن الطيران الحربي التابع للجيش السوداني غارات جوية مكثفة مستهدفاً أعداداً كبيرة من القرى في محيط مدن النهود وغبيش وأبو زبد وود بندة بولاية غرب كردفان، وهي مناطق خاضعة لسيطرة الدعم السريع، ويأتي هذا التصعيد الجوي بالتزامن مع تقدم متسارع يحرزه الجيش تجاه معاقل الدعم السريع في غرب كردفان. وأدى التصعيد الجوي والتقدم المتسارع للجيش إلى إجبار أعداد كبيرة من المدنيين على الفرار نحو إقليم دارفور، بينما فضّل آخرون النزوح نحو مدينة الأبيض بولاية شمال كردفان، بعد نهب الأسواق والمنازل من قبل عناصر الدعم السريع. وقال مرصد كردفان في بيان إن “المواطن صلاح بخيت قُتل إثر إطلاق مسلحين من الدعم السريع النار عليه مباشرة، في منطقة أبو قلب بعد اتهامه بتأييد الجيش، وذلك وفقاً لمعلومات تلقاها المرصد من ناجين”. وأضاف أن مسلحين آخرين قتلوا مواطنين اثنين، هما أبو هشيم محمد وعمر محمد علي، في قرية الشنابلة “الدميرة” المجاورة لمنطقة أبو قلب، قبل أن ينهبوا أبقارهم. وأشار البيان إلى أن الحادثتين وقعتا بالتزامن مع تفاقم الأوضاع الأمنية والإنسانية في المنطقة، التي تعرضت خلال الأسبوع الماضي لقصف جوي مكثف بواسطة طيران الجيش السوداني، أسفر عن مقتل 17 مواطناً على الأقل ونزوح نحو ثلاثة آلاف شخص. واعتبر المرصد استهداف المدنيين وقتلهم ونهب ممتلكاتهم انتهاكاً خطيراً لقواعد القانون الدولي الإنساني، التي تلزم أطراف النزاع بتوفير الحماية للمدنيين وعدم استهدافهم، مشيراً إلى أن هذه الانتهاكات قد ترقى إلى جرائم حرب تستوجب التحقيق والمساءلة. ودعا المنظمات الحقوقية والإنسانية والجهات المعنية إلى رصد الانتهاكات وتوثيقها بصورة مستقلة وحفظ الأدلة تمهيداً لمحاسبة المسؤولين عنها أمام آليات العدالة المحلية والدولية. وطالب بتوفير الحماية العاجلة للمدنيين والنازحين في منطقة أبو قلب، وضمان وصول المساعدات الإنسانية والطبية إلى المصابين والمتضررين. وأبو قلب هي رئاسة وحدة إدارية تتبع لمحلية أبو زبد، وتقع على بعد نحو 17 كيلومتراً شمال شرقي المدينة، وتضم 49 قرية يقدر عدد سكانها الإجمالي بنحو 10 آلاف نسمة. من جانبها، اتهمت غرفة طوارئ دار حمر قوات الدعم السريع بارتكاب مجازر وانتهاكات وصفتها بالوحشية بحق المدنيين في أبو قلب، وقالت إن قائد القوات بالمنطقة حسين برشم حرّض علناً على استهداف السكان على أساس عرقي. وذكرت الغرفة، في نداء استغاثة، أن الانتهاكات شملت عمليات قتل وذبح ونهب وتهجير قسري، مشيرة إلى وقوع عمليات قتل في سوق أبو قلب، إلى جانب تصفية ثلاثة مواطنين رمياً بالرصاص في قرية الدميرة. وأضافت أن الدعم السريع اجتاحت ونهبت قرى “بوزة، جر العسل، حلة أبكر، أولاد مهاجر، سوق الظل، القريش” فضلاً عن عشرات القرى المجاورة. وحذرت الغرفة من موجات نزوح قسري واسعة وتقطع السبل بمئات الأسر في مناطق “قوز حرينديب، أبوجلق، الحمير، الرقيبة، أمدفيس”، مطالبة الجهات المختصة والأجهزة النظامية والمنظمات الحقوقية والإنسانية بالتدخل العاجل لإنقاذ المدنيين والأسر العالقة. الكلمات: أبو زبد أبو قلب أخبار السودان. الأبيض الجيش السوداني السودان النزوح في السودان حقوق الإنسان دار حمر غرب كردفان قوات الدعم السريع مرصد االنيل الازرق «محامو الطوارئ» تحذر من انتقال المعارك إلى الدمازين 21 نوفمبر 2026 في االنيل الازرق , اقاليم , الأخبار , الحرب بين الجيش السوداني والدعم السريع , السودان 0 تحالف الحركة الشعبية والدعم السريع يعلن السيطرة على 5 مناطق جديدة في اقليم النيل الأزرق الدمازين 21 نوفمبر 2026 – حذرت مجموعة محامو الطوارئ، السبت، من مخاطر انتقال العمليات العسكرية إلى مدينة الدمازين، مع تقدم قوات الدعم السريع وحلفائها نحو عاصمة إقليم النيل الأزرق، كاشفة عن رصد أكثر من 130 هجوماً بالطائرات المسيّرة استهدف مناطق متفرقة بالمدينة خلال شهري أكتوبر ونوفمبر الجاريين. وتحرز الدعم السريع تقدماً متسارعاً في جبهة النيل الأزرق جنوب شرق السودان، بعد أن تمكنت خلال الأسبوع الماضي من السيطرة على عدد كبير من البلدات، ما قرّبها أكثر نحو عاصمة النيل الأزرق مدينة الدمازين، وهو ما دفع آلاف المواطنين إلى الفرار نحو ولاية سنار المجاورة. وقالت مجموعة محامو الطوارئ في بيان إن “المجموعة تحذر من المخاطر المتزايدة التي تهدد المدنيين في مدينة الدمازين، حاضرة إقليم النيل الأزرق، في ظل الحشود العسكرية لقوات الدعم السريع وحلفائها وتقدمها نحو المدينة، عقب سيطرتها على عدد من المناطق بالإقليم، مما يثير مخاوف جدية من انتقال العمليات العسكرية إلى المناطق السكنية المكتظة بالمدنيين والنازحين وتعريضهم لانتهاكات جسيمة”. وأوضحت أنها رصدت خلال الشهرين الماضيين أكثر من 130 هجمة بالطائرات المسيّرة على الدمازين، استهدفت منازل سكنية ومحطات وقود ومرافق حيوية وبنى تحتية، مشيرة إلى أن عدد سكان المدينة يُقدر بنحو 400 ألف نسمة، بجانب استقبال المدينة أكثر من 45 ألف نازح جديد خلال العام الجاري، قدموا من محليات الكرمك وقيسان وباو وود الماحي. وحذرت المجموعة من أن امتداد العمليات العسكرية إلى المدينة قد يؤدي إلى سقوط ضحايا بين المدنيين، ووقوع حالات اعتقال تعسفي وعنف جنسي ونهب وتهجير قسري، وتدهور الخدمات الأساسية وتعطيل وصول المساعدات الإنسانية. وفي سياق متصل، أعلنت المجموعة متابعتها مقاطع فيديو متداولة بتاريخ 20 نوفمبر الجاري، تزعم توثيق عمليات تصفية ميدانية لأسرى من القوات المسلحة على أيدي عناصر من الدعم السريع، مؤكدة أنها تعمل على التحقق من صحتها والوقوف على ملابساتها. وقالت إن ثبوت هذه الوقائع يمثل انتهاكاً جسيماً للقانون الدولي الإنساني، الذي يحظر قتل الأسرى والأشخاص العاجزين عن القتال، وقد ترقى هذه الأفعال إلى جرائم حرب تستوجب المساءلة الجنائية. وأعربت المجموعة الحقوقية عن قلقها إزاء تصريحات منسوبة إلى محافظ باو بشأن منع التجار والمدنيين من مغادرة المدينة، محذرة من أن فرض قيود تعسفية على حركة السكان في مناطق النزاع يحرمهم من الوصول إلى مناطق آمنة ويعرض حياتهم للخطر. وطالبت المجموعة قوات الدعم السريع وحلفاءها بوقف الهجمات على المدنيين والأعيان المدنية، وضمان سلامة الأسرى والمحتجزين، ودعت جميع أطراف النزاع إلى احترام حرية حركة المدنيين وتسهيل وصول المساعدات الإنسانية. وناشدت الأمم المتحدة والاتحاد الأفريقي والآليات الدولية المعنية اتخاذ تدابير عاجلة لحماية المدنيين في الدمازين، ومنع وقوع انتهاكات واسعة النطاق، وضمان المساءلة عن الجرائم المرتكبة. الكلمات: أخبار السودان. إقليم النيل الأزرق آخرين من الأسرة. يؤوي المخيم أكثر من 28 ألف نازح، بمن فيهم أشخاص فروا من القتال في وسط كردفان ودارفور. ويوزع برنامج الأغذية العالمي الذرة الرفيعة والزيت النباتي والبقوليات على السكان الأكثر هشاشة. الحين قرابة مليون شخص من دعم الغذاء والتغذية. وخلال أول مهمة ميدانية له إلى السودان بصفته رئيسًا للبرنامج، قال المدير التنفيذي لوك ج. ليندبرغ إن الوكالة لا تستطيع «إطعام الناس أكثر من استمرار النزاع»، نزوح واسعة شملت أهالي 35 قرية، في حين أكدت السلطات المحلية أن الجيش السوداني "يمسك بزمام المبادرة ويتصدى للمهاجمين". وأعلن محافظ محلية باو بولاية النيل الأزرق، عبد الغني دقيس، نزوح سكان 35 قرية بالولاية باتجاه مدينة الدمازين (عاصمة الولاية)، هربا من هجمات قوات الدعم السريع. أخبار مقترحة تسيطر عليه الدعم السريع.. تفاصيل ما يحدث خلف أسوار سجن دقريس بجنوب دارفور الجيش السوداني يصد هجوما على كرنوي ويأسر العشرات من "الدعم السريع" وأوضح دقيس، في تصريحات بثها التلفزيون المحلي، أن قوات الجيش تمكنت من التصدي لهجوم كبير شنته الدعم السريع وألحقت بها الهزيمة، مؤكدا أن الجيش طارد تلك القوات إلى السريع بتعمد "ارتكاب انتهاكات واسعة شملت السرقة والنهب والاغتصاب". الجيش يمسك بالمبادرة وعلى الصعيد الميداني أيضا، قلّلت السلطات السودانية في الولاية من تداعيات الهجوم، مؤكدة أن الجيش يمسك بزمام المبادرة ويعمل على استعادة الأمن في المناطق الجنوبية. وجاءت هذه التطمينات على لسان المتحدث باسم حكومة النيل الأزرق، سيف النصر من الله محمود، في أعقاب إعلان قوات الدعم السريع فرض سيطرتها على 5 مناطق المواطنين، لكنه أوضح أن "الحرب كرّ وفرّ، والأمر على أرض الواقع ليس كما يُشاع في مواقع التواصل الاجتماعي". ودعا المتحدث المواطنين إلى الهدوء والوقوف خلف القوات المسلحة، مؤكدا وجود تنسيق كامل بين القيادتين السياسية والعسكرية لدحر قوات الدعم السريع وإعادة الاستقرار للولاية. شاهد 3:09 3:09 حراك دبلوماسي أمريكي سياسيا، أجرى وزير الخارجية الأمريكي ماركو روبيو ، أمس الجمعة، اتصالا هاتفيا مع نائب للتوصل إلى هدنة إنسانية، وتحقيق سلام دائم، إلى جانب الانتقال إلى مسار الحكومة المدنية. وتأتي هذه المباحثات في سياق تحركات وجهود إقليمية ودولية تسعى للتوصل إلى وقف شامل لإطلاق النار، وإطلاق عملية 21 نوفمبر 2026 • تحديث : 21 نوفمبر 2026 الأرشيف SUDAN الخرطوم/ عادل عبد الرحيم/ الأناضول أعلن محافظ محلية باو بولاية النيل الأزرق جنوب شرقي السودان عبد الغني دقيس، مساء الجمعة، نزوح أهالي 35 قرية بالولاية، جراء هجمات قوات الدعم السريع. وقال المحافظ في تصريحات بثها التلفزيون المحلي بولاية النيل الأزرق، إن قوات الجيش تصدت لهجوم كبير من قوات الدعم السريع، واستطاعت هزيمتها. وأضاف: "الأحوال هادئة تماماً في المحافظة اليوم الجمعة". ولفت المحافظ إلى أن "أهالي 35 قرية نزحوا إلى مدينة الدمازين (عاصمة الولاية)"، دون تحديد عدد النازحين. وحذر من أن "عددا من الأطفال والنساء وكبار السن لا يزالون في الطرقات، والدعم السريع يعمدون إلى السرقة والنهب والاغتصاب". المحافظ أكد أن الجيش طارد قوات الدعم السريع إلى جنوب باو. وفي وقت سابق الجمعة، أعلن المتحدث باسم حكومة النيل الأزرق (المحلية) سيف النصر من الله محمود، أن الجيش يمسك بزمام المبادرة ويعمل على استعادة الأمن في جنوب الولاية. جاء ذلك بعد ساعات من إعلان "قوات الدعم السريع"، فرض سيطرتها على 5 مناطق بولاية النيل الأزرق، وهي خور ماك، والمدينة 10، والمدينة 11، وسنجة نبق، وقرية الطاقة، دون تعقيب فوري من الجيش. وتبعد هذه المناطق عن الدمازين بمسافات لا تتجاوز 80 كيلومترا. والخميس، أعلنت قوات الدعم السريع، في بيان، سيطرتها على "مدينة 12، ومنطقة ديرنق"، بعد معارك مع القوات الحكومية. وفي اليوم ذاته، أعلن الجيش تنفيذ عملية عسكرية في ديرنق، وتدمير 28 عربة قتالية والاستيلاء على 18 أخرى من قوات الدعم السريع. وتشهد ولاية النيل الأزرق تصعيداً عسكرياً خلال الأيام الماضية، على خلفية شن قوات الدعم السريع والحركة الشعبية/شمال المتحالفة معها هجمات على عدة مناطق بالولاية. وتتفاقم المعاناة الإنسانية في السودان جراء الحرب بين الجيش وقوات الدعم السريع، المستمرة منذ أبريل/نيسان 2023، بسبب خلاف بشأن توحيد المؤسسة العسكرية، ما أسفر عن مقتل عشرات الآلاف ونزوح نحو 13 مليون شخص. news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription باتت منطقة بكوري مسرحاً جديداً لاستخدام «الكيماوي» من قبل الجيش. أدلة جديدة وتحصلت «العين الإخبارية» على أدلة جديدة تُثبت تورط الجيش السوداني في استخدام السلاح الكيماوي خلال المعارك الحربية الدائرة الآن في ولاية النيل الأزرق، خصوصاً في منطقة بكوري بالقرب من الدماذين. وأدلت المحامية والناشطة الحقوقية المدافعة عن حقوق الإنسان في السودان، رحاب المبارك سيد أحمد، بمعلومات جديدة لـ«العين الإخبارية»، أكدت فيها استمرار الجيش السوداني في استخدام السلاح الكيماوي رغم كل الضغوط التي مورست عليه من قبل مؤسسات المجتمع الدولي. وقالت سيد أحمد: "إن شهودًا من الميدان ومن منطقة الدمازين تحديدا، أكدوا أن رئيس هيئة الأركان في الجيش السوداني، الفريق ياسر العطا، و رئيس الحركة الشعبية شمال في النيل الأزرق مالك عقار، قاما وقبل عدة أسابيع، بنقل أسلحة ورؤوس وقنابل كيميائية إلى المنطقة العسكرية بالفرقة الرابعة مشاة بالدمازين». وأضافت، أن «الشاهد الذي أشارت إليه بالحروف (ي.ف) لدواعٍ أمنية، ذكر أن المعركة التي دارت بين الجيش السوداني والدعم السريع في صبيحة يوم 5 نوفمبر/ تشرين الثاني الجاري، قام فيها الجيش السوداني، وقبيل انسحابه من منطقة بكوري، بقصف قنابل الكلور الكيميائية في مواجهة قوات الدعم السريع، وأن الاستخدام المباشر لغاز الكلور أثر بصورة مباشرة على المدنيين الذين يسكنون المنطقة، خاصة وأن المنطقة العسكرية باللواء 13 تقع وسط المناطق السكنية». وكانت قوات الدعم السريع، سيطرت في 5 نوفمبر/تشرين الثاني الجاري، على منطقة بكوري للمرة الثانية، من الجيش الذي سبق وسيطر عليها في 22 أكتوبر/ تشرين الأول الماضي. وتابعت الناشطة الحقوقية، نقلاً عن الشاهد: إن أغلب سكان بكوري شاهدوا أقنعة الوجه التي يرتديها عناصر الجيش السوداني عادة أثناء استخدامهم لقنابل غاز الكلور، تملأ المكان بعد انسحابهم». وأضافت أن «هذا المشهد هو الذي جعل السكان يؤكدون حقيقة استخدام السلاح الكيماوي، خاصة بعد إصابة أغلبهم بحرقة وغشاوة شديدة أثناء النظر خلال النهار، وبعدم الرؤية تمامًا في الليل، إضافة إلى الالتهابات الشديدة والتضخم في الحبال الصوتية». فرار جماعي وأكد الشاهد الذي اعتمدت عليه الناشطة الحقوقية رحاب المبارك في معلوماتها التي أدلت بها لـ"العين الإخبارية"، أن الجزء القليل من أهالي المنطقة الذي يملك المال يتلقى العلاج حاليًا في مستشفى (أصوصا) الإثيوبية، بينهم المواطن (ش.د) المصاب في عينيه وحباله الصوتية، وكذلك المواطن (م.د). بينما الغالبية العظمى من المدنيين الذين لا يملكون المال، بينهم: المواطنة (ك.م) ٣٠ عامًا والمواطن (م.ي) والمواطن (ع.ك)، يتلقون علاجا بدائيا، مثل: الملح والقرض والليمون وعروق الأشجار. الشاهد ‏(ي. ف‏)، أكد أن أغلب سكان بكوري هربوا بسبب الحرب الدائرة والسموم الكيميائية التي تملأ المنطقة إلى الدمازين، مشيرًا إلى أن جزءا منهم وصل إلى (قيسان) و(ديم سعد) و(يارا) و(أشمبوا)، وهي مناطق تقع في أقاصي النيل الأزرق. وقالت رحاب لـ"العين الإخبارية": إن "مواصلة الجيش السوداني لاستخدام السلاح الكيميائي أثناء حربه مع الدعم السريع جريمة حرب نكراء، تستوجب التحري العاجل من منظمة حظر الأسلحة الكيميائية بعد أن ثبت وبالأدلة امتلاكه لقنابل قام بمعالجتها محليًا مستخدمًا فيها غاز الكلور المحرم دوليًا"، على حد قولها. معارك النيل الأزرق وتشهد ولاية النيل الأزرق في الحدود الجنوب شرقية للسودان، معارك عنيفة بين الجيش السوداني وقوات الدعم السريع التي تقاتل ضمن تحالف السودان التأسيسي "تأسيس" في هذه الولاية تحديداً. وذكرت تقارير محلية بأن قوات تأسيس سيطرت على منطقة "باو" الاستراتيجية أقرب مناطق النيل الأزرق للدماذين. فضلا عن تقارير أخرى تتحدث عن حالة تراجع وانسحابات لقوات الجيش السوداني إلى خارج نطاق ولاية النيل الأزرق. وبحسب بيان صادر الجمعة، عن قوات تأسيس اطلعت عليه "العين الإخبارية"، فإن "قوات تحالف السودان التأسيسي «تأسيس»، قالت إنها تمكنت، من تحرير 5 مناطق بإقليم النيل الأزرق - الفونج الجديد (خور ماك، المدينة 10، المدينة 11، سنجة نبق، وقرية الطاقة)وسط حالة من الانهيار في صفوف جيش الحركة الإسلامية". وأضافت: أن قواتنا سوف تعمل على ضمان حماية المدنيين، وتأمين الأسواق والمرافق العامة، وإعادة فتح الأسواق والخدمات الأساسية للمواطنين في جميع المناطق التي تم تحريرها". ماذا نعرف عن بكوري؟ بكوري منطقة سكانية بسيطة تبعد حوالي 70 كيلو مترا عن مدينة الدماذين حاضرة ولاية النيل الأزرق. ويعمل معظم سكانها في الزراعة والحرف البسيطة. وبمنطقة بكوري يوجد اللواء 13 الذي يتبع للفرقة الرابعة مشاة التابعة للجيش السوداني بالدمازين. السودان غرفة الأخبار #حوارات_العين_الإخبارية رئاسة «الاتحادي» اختيار المحرر نجل الميرغني الأكبر مرشداً للختمية وإرجاء حسم رئاسة «الاتحادي» 20 نوفمبر 2026 في اختيار المحرر , الأخبار , السودان , سياسة 0 السيد علي محمد عثمان الميرغني - صورة ارشيفية الخرطوم 20 نوفمبر 2026 – أعلنت أسرة الراحل محمد عثمان الميرغني، زعيم السجادة الختمية والحزب الاتحادي الديمقراطي الأصل، تنصيب نجله الأكبر “السيد علي” مرشداً للطريقة الختمية. في الأثناء، ما زال منصب رئيس الحزب الاتحادي الديمقراطي غير محسوم، في ظل توقعات باحتدام التنافس حول المنصب بين نجلي الميرغني “السيد محمد الحسن والسيد جعفر الصادق”. وتلا جعفر الصادق الميرغني خطاب الأسرة الميرغنية الخاص بتنصيب المرشد الجديد للطريقة الختمية قائلاً: “فقد منّ الله على المسلمين بأن اجتمعت كلمة الأسرة، واجتمع الأمر، بحمد الله، بتقديم أخي الأكبر لمقام المرشد.. فقد تقرر تقديم شيخي وسيدي وأخي الأكبر، مولانا السيد علي السيد محمد عثمان الميرغني، مرشداً للختمية، خلفاً لوالدنا وشيخنا الإمام المجدد مولانا السيد محمد عثمان الميرغني”. وتابع قائلاً: “أنا وإخوتي جميعاً أول من يقف خلفه، ونشد أزره، ونضع أيدينا في يده على خدمة الطريق وأهله”. ودعا المرشد الجديد في أول خطاب له أنصار الطائفة الختمية، إلى إدارة الخلافات بالحوار والاستماع لوجهات النظر ونبذ الفرقة وتأييد أي مسعى للصلح وجمع الكلمة. ويقيم السيد علي الميرغني المرشد الجديد للختمية في الولايات المتحدة الأمريكية منذ منتصف التسعينات. وكان الموت غيّب السيد محمد عثمان الميرغني يوم الجمعة الماضي بالقاهرة، ووُوري الثرى بمسجد السيد علي الميرغني بالخرطوم بحري الإثنين الماضي. وبتنصيب نجل الراحل “السيد علي” مرشداً للطريقة الختمية، تكون زعامة إحدى أكبر الطوائف الدينية في السودان قد حُسمت، لكن تبقى رئاسة الحزب الاتحادي الديمقراطي الأصل مثاراً لخلاف متوقع. وعلى حياة الراحل محمد عثمان الميرغني، نشب الخلاف بين نجليه – الحسن وجعفر – على منصب الرجل الثاني في الحزب، وهو منصب نائب رئيس الحزب لشؤون التنظيم. وتشير “سودان تربيون” إلى أن من محفزات الخلاف بين الطرفين موقف الحسن القريب من القوى المدنية الرافضة للحرب، وموقف جعفر المناصر للجيش في حربه ضد قوات الدعم السريع. الكلمات: أخبار السودان. الحزب الاتحادي الديمقراطي الأصل الخرطوم بحري الطريقة الختمية جعفر The author (file photo) Aklog Birara (Dr) Executive summary Ethiopia’s experience since 2018 is not a simple story of a peace prize followed by war. It is a story of an initially promising opening that did not resolve deeper struggles over political legitimacy, The newly appointed Prime Minister of Ethiopia Abiy Ahmed Ali managed to do two things simultaneously: charmed Ethiopians and the international community presenting himself and his party as reformists; and b) dismantled national institutions systematically and replaced them with Oromo elites and beneficiaries. This state capture changed the distribution of power, income and wealth, security arrangements, identity, land, and accountability. By all measurements on the ground concerning human life and wellbeing, Abiy Ahmed Ali is a murderer/genocider. Bloodletting of civilians he considers unworthy of life does not bother him. He undermines peace and democracy deliberately and systematically. Abiy Ahmed Ali suffers from a distorted mindset of grievance redress by punishing his enemies and opponents, slaughtering, starving, displacing, harassing, jailing primarily Amhara and Tigrayans (Abyssinians or northerners) by any means necessary. The costs are enormous. Accountability matters Abiy Ahmed Ali and partners must be held accountable for war crimes, crimes against humanity and ethnic cleansing. Ethiopia will never enjoy peace without accountability. The institutional and structural changes taking place under the watch of Abiy Ahmed Ali are dramatic and irreversible. Think of the replacement of Ethiopia with Oromia; think of the change in the redesignation of Addis Ababa as Finfinnee. Think of Afan Oromo replacing Amharic as Ethiopia’s official language. There is nothing the international community would do if these were to occur. The 2018 rapprochement with Eritrea was a genuine diplomatic achievement. Yet the 2020–22 Tigray war, continuing violence in Oromia and the conflict in Amhara since 2023 reveal how fragile a settlement becomes when adversaries do not trust institutions or believe they can protect their interests peacefully. Root causes remain intact. The 2022 Pretoria agreement stopped a major phase of warfare but did not settle all underlying disputes or include all directly affected constituencies. [1–5] A viable peace process must therefore do more than obtain another ceasefire. It needs enforceable civilian-protection commitments, inclusive negotiation, independent monitoring, credible justice, space for peaceful political competition, and a negotiated approach to contested constitutional and territorial questions. No community should have to accept collective punishment, and no armed actor including the ruling party should be exempt from scrutiny. The single most critical hurdle to lasting peace and stability in Ethiopia is the Abiy ruling party and state. It is intolerant of peace and stability. It thrives on division. conflict and war. It breeds animosity and fear among ethnic and faith groups. It compromises Ethiopia’s sovereign interests by submitting itself to the UAE and its regional national goals. How does one explain Abiy Ahmed’s strategic partnership with Sudan’ s RSF? With the UAE? Why peace is illusive in Ethiopia. From the promise of 2018 to recurrent conflict Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in April 2018 and initiated reforms, including political prisoner releases and an opening of civic space. The Nobel Peace Prize in 2019 recognized particularly his role in the rapprochement with Eritrea, not a finding that Ethiopia had achieved lasting internal peace. The Nobel committee itself acknowledged the difficulty of democratization and continuing internal conflicts. [1] The question posed to the Nobel Committee is why a peace prize without demonstrated commitment to permanent peace and democratization? The transition unfolded amid longstanding grievances over centralized authority, ethnically organized federalism, political exclusion, competing territorial claims and unequal perceptions of security. Conflict between the federal government and the TPLF escalated into war in November 2020. The war involved federal, Tigrayan, Eritrean and regional forces, and devastated communities across Tigray, Amhara and Afar. The African Union-mediated Pretoria cessation-of-hostilities agreement of November 2022 reduced the fighting but left disputes over territory, displacement, implementation, and accountability unresolved. [2, 3, 6] The AU failed to demand inclusion of critical stakeholders: Afar and Amhara. In Amhara, tensions over the Pretoria process, territorial claims, and the April 2023 plan to dismantle regional special forces contributed to a confrontation between federal forces and Fano formations. In Oromia, armed conflict involving the Oromo Liberation Army and government forces persisted, accompanied by allegations of serious abuses against civilians. These conflicts have different histories; treating them as one undifferentiated rebellion obscures what each settlement must address. [2, 4, 7] Left with a sense of impunity, the Abiy government continued its assaults on civilians in the Afar. Amhara, Gambella, Oromia, Somali and Tigray regions. The latest flare between Oromo and Somali regional forces with the complicity of federal forces forced tens of thousands to flee to Kenya. In effect, Abiy Ahmed’s war is no longer confined to the Amhara and Tigray regions . It is national and regional. What the evidence shows about the democratic deficit. Freedom House’s 2026 assessment classifies Ethiopia as “Not Free,” scoring it eighteen out of one hundred, and identifies restrictions on political competition, media, civil society, due process, and independent institutions. Its Freedom on the Net report identifies connectivity restrictions in conflict-affected areas, including Amhara. These are assessments by an independent monitoring organization, not a legal determination that every government action is unlawful. [4, 8] Human Rights Watch’s World Report 2026 describes continued armed conflict, serious abuses by warring parties, and restrictions on civic space. The UN International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia documented serious violations and abuses by multiple parties during the northern war, including war crimes and crimes against humanity. Responsibility for incidents must still be assessed on evidence, with individual accountability rather than collective blame. [2, 5] 3 | Why peace has remained elusive: Competing claims of political legitimacy Many political constituencies disagree not only about who should govern but about the rules of the state itself: the balance of federal and regional authority, the rights of individuals and communities, the electoral system, and the status of disputed territories. Without trusted procedures for resolving those questions, every major policy dispute can become a security crisis. In huge part, the reason is because Abiy Ahmed Ali has Oromoized the state and government. Non-Oromo are subject to alienation, marginalization, and submission. The option left is to defend their sheer survival. Security dilemmas and coercive disarmament When communities fear that, surrendering arms leaves them vulnerable, disarmament without credible guarantees can intensify insecurity. Conversely, the proliferation of armed forces undermines civilian authority and exposes communities to abuse. Sequenced, independently verified security arrangements are essential; neither unconditional coercion nor indefinite militarization offers a stable solution. Incomplete peace agreements and excluded stakeholders Pretoria demonstrated that negotiation could stop large-scale fighting. It also illustrates the limits of a deal that does not settle implementation, return of displaced people, disputed boundaries, and the security concerns of other affected actors. Durable arrangements must incorporate local communities, women, displaced persons, and civil society—not only the signatories who command fighters. [3, 6] Pretoria is flawed because it is not inclusive. Impunity, civilian harm, and collapsing trust Allegations of unlawful killings, arbitrary detention, attacks on health care, abductions and abuses by both state and non-state actors deepen grievances and discourage reconciliation. Independent investigations, survivor-centered remedies, and fair trials are necessary to break cycles of retaliation. The absence of trusted justice also makes ceasefires difficult to sustain. [2, 5] Humanitarian distress and regional spillover Displacement, damaged health and education systems, insecurity along transport routes, and constraints on relief access compound the political crisis. Relations with Eritrea and Sudan and disputes across the Horn of Africa add external incentives and risks. A November 2026 U.S. A Congressional Research Service report warns that overlapping rebellions and regional tensions could fuel a wider confrontation; such risk analysis should not be confused with a prediction that war is inevitable. [3, 9] The United Arab Emirates is a major component of the Ethiopian crisis. The international community must sanction this state actor that supplies drones and other weapons to Abiy’s army that in turn uses these weapons to slaughter civilians like chickens. The UAE is a destabilizing force in Africa. Independent domestic and international observers question “ Why Ethiopian elites fail to work together, do the needful and propose viable solutions with a timeframe” is baffling. What Ethiopians together can do: a practical peace architecture. First 90 days: protect lives and create a credible opening. Announce and independently monitor reciprocal civilian-protection commitments: no attacks on civilians, schools, clinics, aid workers, or civilian infrastructure; publish incident-reporting channels and rapid investigation procedures. Negotiate localized humanitarian pauses and safe access routes, with UN, Red Cross and trusted Ethiopian relief organizations assessing needs impartially across Amhara, Oromia, Tigray, Afar and other affected areas. Begin confidential exploratory talks involving federal authorities and relevant armed and civilian representatives; establish mutually acceptable mediators and guarantees against retaliation for peaceful participation. Release people arbitrarily detained, protect journalists and civil society monitors, restore communications where restricted, and enable independent observation subject to lawful security safeguards. Three to twelve months: negotiate and verify. Create an inclusive national peace forum with meaningful participation by women, youth, religious leaders, professional associations, displaced communities, minority groups, and diaspora voices; participation must not be equated with endorsing any armed group. Agree on phased ceasefires and security arrangements, with transparent benchmarks for troop repositioning, demobilization, reintegration, local policing, and protection of vulnerable populations. Establish independent, survivor-centered mechanisms for documentation, truth-seeking, reparations and prosecution of serious crimes, with safeguards for witness security and due process. Launch technical commissions on contested territories, federal-regional powers, land rights, and electoral rules; defer final decisions to legitimate constitutional and democratic procedures rather than military victory. One to three years: institutionalize peace. Strengthen electoral administration, judicial independence, parliamentary oversight and protections for opposition parties, media, and civil society. Rebuild public services and livelihoods using transparent needs-based allocations, audited funds, and community oversight; prioritize displaced people’s voluntary, safe and dignified return, or other durable solutions. Develop shared civic education and cross-community dialogue that recognize the suffering of Amhara, Oromo, Tigrayan, Afar, Somali, and other Ethiopian civilians without competitive victimhood. Secure regional non-interference commitments and international support for verification and reconstruction, while keeping Ethiopian communities central to decisions. 5 | Who must contribute—and what they can commit to. Federal institutions: uphold constitutional and humanitarian obligations, enable independent monitoring, negotiate in good faith, and accept impartial accountability. Armed groups: halt attacks on civilians, permit humanitarian access, reject forced recruitment, and participate in verifiable security talks. Political parties and regional administrations: pursue claims through nonviolent, transparent processes. Religious and community leaders: provide trusted spaces for dialogue without silencing victims. Diaspora organizations: support documented advocacy, relief, and bridge-building rather than dehumanizing rhetorical hold vigils and protests and highlight the tragedy inflicted on ordinary citizens by their own government that is supposed to protect them. In this connection, the protests consisting of members of the Horn of Africa in Washington on November 16 as well as those in Minnesota that issued a strong statement calling on the international community to hold the government of Ethiopia accountable are remarkable and encouraging developments. International partners: support mediation, needs-based aid, and independent accountability without imposing a political outcome. How to measure whether a peace process is real Public monthly indicators should include civilian deaths and injuries independently documented; safe humanitarian access and assistance delivered; school and clinic functionality; verified ceasefire violations; numbers of displaced people accessing voluntary durable solutions; arbitrary detention cases reviewed; participation of women and displaced communities in talks; and implementation of agreed security and justice milestones. A peace announcement without measurable improvement in civilian safety is insufficient. Conclusions Abiy Ahmed’s OPDO dominance and reconfiguration of the Ethiopian State notwithstanding, Ethiopia’s crisis cannot be explained solely by one leader, one ethnicity or one-armed movement. It is the entire system that must be overhauled. Decisions by political and military leaders’ matter, but the deeper challenge is the absence of trusted, enforceable rules for resolving disagreement. The 2018 opening showed that change is possible; the wars that followed show that ethnic elite dominated diplomacy without inclusive institutions is fragile. Assessing and critiquing the OPDO-dominated Prosperity Party is important but not enough. Ethiopia cannot afford to suffer from a mental model of permanent war. It is not a win-win model at all. It is a choice Aby Ahmed has chosen, but not for the benefit and wellbeing of the Ethiopian people. Equally, the Amhara Fano National Movement has an obligation to assess its institutional and leadership strengths and weaknesses and renew itself. The leadership must also evaluate the value added of the newly formed Alliance for Survival. Whose agenda is this new entity advancing? Long-term Ethiopians can build a more durable peace by insisting on good and democratic governance that guarantees equal civilian protection, accountable government, nonviolent political competition, genuine representation, and practical agreements whose implementation can be verified. There is no evidence that the Abiy regime is ready and willing to democratize Ethiopia. The choice of constitutional arrangements and political leadership belongs to Ethiopians through peaceful, rights-respecting processes. This is the reason a Pan-Ethiopian platform to discuss the elephant in the room–why no peace and democracy? – is essential. Finally, this author believes Ethiopians together must push for an all-inclusive series of conferences at the earliest opportunity. Ethiopian News November 20, 2026 Updated: November 20, 2026 Ten Killed in Attack on Gold Mining Site and Special Forces Patrol in Bero Woreda November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber Nine regional special forces members and a security guard were killed during an armed assault in Ethiopia’s Southwest Ethiopia Peoples’ Region. By Staff Writer (Nairobi, Kenya) — Armed attackers killed nine regional special forces personnel and a gold mining company security guard in Bero woreda, Southwest Ethiopia Peoples’ Region, on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, according to residents, eyewitnesses, and Deutsche Welle (DW). Eyewitnesses told DW that armed assailants targeted a gold mining site in the Chilema Shet area of Garo kebele on Wednesday morning, November 18, 2026. The attackers killed a security guard and burned company staff quarters alongside vehicles, including bulldozers and graders. One eyewitness who fled the scene stated that attackers killed special forces members attempting to defend the site. Eyewitness accounts reported by DW indicate that regional special forces traveled toward Chilema Shet from Jeba town, the administrative seat of Bero woreda, after the attack began. Assailants ambushed their patrol vehicle on the road. Nine of the ten special forces members on board died, while one survived with injuries. A relative of one victim told DW that families received the bodies of the slain personnel for burial on Wednesday and Thursday, November 19, 2026. DW reported that Bero woreda Chief Administrator Gemeda Kayidadi declined to comment. Peace and security officials in the West Omo Zone and the Southwest Ethiopia Region did not respond to phone calls seeking comment. West Omo Zone—a predominantly pastoralist area bordering South Sudan—has experienced recurring insecurity, with past attacks claiming the lives of foreign visitors, local residents, and security personnel. Ethiopian News November 20, 2026 Updated: November 20, 2026 U.S. Issues Travel Alert as Border Clashes and Troop Build-Up Heighten Ethiopia-Eritrea War Fears, Reports November 20, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber Rising tensions and artillery fire along the border prompt a U.S. travel warning as Ethiopian and Eritrean forces mass near Badme File/SM By Staff Writer (Nairobi, Kenya) — Heavy troop deployments, artillery exchanges, and cross-border clashes along the Ethiopia-Eritrea frontier have raised fears of a wider war, prompting the U.S. Embassy in Ethiopia to issue a security warning to its citizens, according to BBC Amharic and international reports. In a warning issued on Thursday, November 19, 2026, the U.S. Embassy urged Americans to reconsider travel to Ethiopia. The embassy advised against travel to the Tigray, Amhara, and Afar regions—specifically highlighting southern Afar and rural border areas of Tigray—and called on U.S. citizens in those areas to leave while safe to do so. BBC Amharic reported that the alert follows assessments from international outlets, including AFP and Reuters on November 18, 2026, indicating that Ethiopia and Eritrea stand on the brink of war as forces position themselves at close range along the border. Citing the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED) and sources linked to armed groups, Reuters reported direct military exchanges in recent days. AFP cited analysts and foreign security sources pointing to heavy weapons attacks, cross-border incursions, and military preparations on the Ethiopian side. ACLED reported that Eritrean troops redeployed to the Badme area last week after pulling back in mid-October, massing soldiers and heavy equipment in Gwal Gemhalo and Simbel. Meanwhile, Ethiopian forces deployed close to the front line and fired heavy artillery toward positions near Badme, a contested flashpoint of the 1998–2000 war. Accounts of the fighting remain disputed. A source close to a pro-government militia in Tigray rejected reports of direct clashes with Eritrean forces. Eritrea’s Minister of Information, Yemane Gebremeskel, dismissed reports of border tensions as Ethiopian ruling-party propaganda without addressing troop deployments or fighting directly. Residents in Tigray’s North West Zone—including in Shiraro, Adi Hageray, and Biyara—told BBC Amharic that fighting involving artillery and drones pushed into rural areas earlier in the month, displacing border residents. Local officials, medical sources, and BBC Amharic accounts also reported that a drone strike in Biyara kebele near Badme on Monday, November 16, 2026, wounded at least four civilians riding in a white Isuzu pickup truck. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara have deteriorated sharply following Ethiopia’s push for sea access, mutual accusations involving armed groups, and severed diplomatic ties. Surging fuel costs have directly raised agricultural input expenses, notably driving up fertilizer prices. This inflation lowers crop yields and reduces purchasing power for both rural and urban households. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: PM Abiy Welcomes Global Health Leaders to Cphia 2026 in Addis Ababa - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: PM Abiy Welcomes Global Health Leaders to Cphia 2026 in Addis Ababa 20 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has invited African leaders, health experts, and global partners to Addis Ababa for the Fifth International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2026), calling for collective action to build a healthier and more resilient continent. In a video message shared on social media, the Prime Minister announced that Ethiopia will host the conference from November 23 to 27 at the Addis International Convention Center. The event will be co-hosted by Ethiopia and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC). Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The conference is expected to bring together heads of state, ministers, researchers, innovators, and development partners to strengthen continental cooperation and advance African-led solutions to public health challenges, he said. PM Abiy said Ethiopia was proud to host the important gathering and looking forward to welcoming leaders, researchers, and partners from across Africa and beyond. The conference provides an important opportunity to unite knowledge, strengthen partnerships, and advance African-led solutions to the continent's health priorities, the Prime Minister underscored. "Together, let us turn shared aspirations into collective action and build a healthier, more resilient Africa," the Prime Minister underscored, adding, "Africa is ready." Held under the theme "Africa's Health Security and Sovereignty," CPHIA 2026 will focus on reducing external dependence in the health sector, strengthening resilient healthcare systems, and advancing African ownership of public health priorities. ethiopia.title: Tigray's Unfinished Struggle - From Historical Betrayal to Self-Determination
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Tigray's Unfinished Struggle - From Historical Betrayal to Self-Determination - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Tigray's Unfinished Struggle - From Historical Betrayal to Self-Determination 20 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) opinion By Negasi Awetehey Addis Abeba — Tigray's dynamic relationship with the modern Ethiopian state has been shaped by a historical paradox and contradiction: Tigray has been both a target of state oppression, betrayal, and genocide and, at critical moments, an influential participant in shaping the Ethiopian state itself. The Meles Zenawi era brought a long-awaited sense of relief and ecstasy to the people of Tigray after years of struggle, suffering, and uncertainty. This shift from prolonged agony to renewed hope was captured in the title of the late Dr. Solomon Enkuay's book, The Agony and Ecstasy of Tigray --a title that evokes historical contradictions: the enduring pain of oppression and conflict, alongside the exhilaration of hard-won political transformation and a new social contract. Under the EPRDF-led Ethiopian state, the people of Tigray were encouraged to believe in a shared identity founded on self-determination, equality, and mutual respect. Placing uncritical faith in the Ethiopian state, Tigrayans prioritized peace, development, and coexistence, often at the expense of safeguarding Tigray's long-term benefits. Today, that trust has been shattered, leaving behind a profound sense of collective betrayal. The promise of equality, mutual respect, and unity in diversity has become an illusion. Hated throughout history, yet ever-present Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The land of Tigray has witnessed some of the most frequent and brutal battles in human history. Millennial before the formation of Ethiopia, Tigray endured wars. Before the 2020 war, I used to hear elders saying more than 30 battles had been fought in Tigray. Figures from the center to dehumanize, especially driven by the hate of the 1970s/80s TPLF movement in the north but Tigrayans, manipulate and label it ' ሰሜኑ ሁሌ ጦርነት: የተረገመ ምድር' (the north is always at war: the cursed land). From an archaeological perspective, the earliest destruction dates back to the D'mt period (5th century BC). This was destruction of monumental temples and palaces an era when there was no world order, security and sovereignty, when a powerful empire from afar could invade any group or polity at will. Tigray, even in the age of world order and sovereignty, has endured foreign invasions and wars. Ethiopia's political sovereignty has done little to ensure the security and sovereignty of the Tigray people. Leaving ancient conflicts aside, modern wars in Tigray have put the state acting as either an indifferent or an aggressor or in alliance with the foreign forces. There was also a process that, under the guise of nation-building, the Ethiopian state fractured Tigray's territory and stripped its autonomy and capacity--deliberately leaving it weak and vulnerable to foreign invasion and internal suppression. Because the agency is in the hands of the Ethiopian state, and the same agency adding other foreign agencies has been used to invade Tigray. The 2020-2022 war waged against Tigray by the Prosperity Party-led Ethiopia demonstrates that one hardly needs to study history to witness this ugliest repetition. This government's attempt to decimate Tigray brought Eritrean forces and other drone powers with geopolitical interests. History repeats itself, but each repetition grows uglier. Another unsettling pattern for Tigray is that the broader Ethiopian populace within the country's map is not aware of Ethiopia's sovereignty and the dignity of its people. Instead, they have been manipulated into aligning with foreign forces to annihilate their own fraternal neighbor, Tigray. Meresa Tsehaye, a scholar of political science and security studies, underscores Tigray's dual position as a historically marginalized periphery within the modern Ethiopian state and a strategic part of the wider Horn of Africa. Caught between regional rivalries and competing geopolitical interests, Tigray remains vulnerable to the ambitions of global powers, Middle Eastern actors, and East African states. These overlapping geopolitical, geo-cultural, and geostrategic dynamics risk perpetuating Tigray's role as a hotspot of regional instability, where external interests overshadow its people's rights, security, and aspirations. The recurring cycle of invasion underscores the imperative of a sovereign future for Tigray. The only way to prevent war--the ugliest reality Tigrayans have abhorred throughout history, yet one that remains ever-present--is to secure the future and sovereignty. The Ethiopian government's war on Tigray started in 2020 but has never stopped. The exercise of Tigray's right to self-determination has been pushed aside. Unless this trajectory is reversed, Tigray faces the risk of being erased from the map and its people being wiped out. If this is not possible, political subjugation and assimilation remain the likely scenarios. Reversing this course is imperative for Tigray to safeguard its people, restore their dignity, and secure their right to determine their own future. Existential incompatibility of PP Ideology, Tigray nationalism The relationship between the PP's ideology and Tigrayan identity is fundamentally defined by a profound asymmetry: that between the perpetrator and the victim of betrayal, genocide, and violence. Their relationship is characterized by a fundamental contradiction--one resembling that between the killer and the killed, the perpetrator and the victim, or the betrayer and the betrayed. Although the word "Prosperity" ostensibly evokes progress, growth, and development, it has acquired an altogether different and deeply pejorative meaning in the popular consciousness of Tigray. Through a bitter linguistic play on words, Prosperity (ብልጽግና) has been recast as ብዕልግና (Biligina) in Tigrigna--a term associated with vulgarity, moral corruption, and misconduct. Consequently, Tigrayans who chose to align themselves with or join the PP came to be branded ባዕሊጉ (Baeligu), a charged label that, in this context, conveys profound condemnation of what is perceived as a betrayal of collective values, dignity, and solidarity. The post-Pretoria chapter was supposed to prove if the Prosperity Party had anything to offer Tigray--peace, justice, restoration, or rehabilitation. Instead, Tigray stood amidst ruin: over 600,000 killed, millions displaced , and its essential health, education, and transport infrastructure systematically looted and destroyed. Rather than repairing this damage , the regime has launched a new campaign to finish what it started and conquer the region completely. Ultimately, the ruling party has put nothing on Tigray's table except death or subjugation. The choice before Tigray is not simply between competing political arrangements ..." Across all phases of the war, Tigray's heritage--ancient and modern, sacred and secular--was targeted in a deliberate attempt to break a nation's spirit. From medieval monasteries to modern museums and historic icons, the assault aimed directly at what Tigrayans hold as their living soul. This physical destruction works hand-in-hand with historical abuse: through epistemic erasure, historiographical hegemony, and revisionist appropriation, ruling party figures seek to rewrite the legacy that their ethnic base belongs to the ancient legacy and history in Tigray. It is a dual-pronged strategy of cultural erasure and historical theft--destroying a people's living identity while co-opting their ancient legacy to legitimize the incumbent's party authority. Ultimately, the Prosperity Party's strategy is designed to weaken and depopulate substantive political entities like Tigray, replacing legitimate regional leadership with subservient proxies to entrench OPDO (currently, Oromo Prosperity Party) political and economic dominance. By attempting to project power into strategic maritime corridors like Assab, the ruling apparatus seeks to consolidate indefinite and irreversible rule--a centralized trajectory that is fundamentally incompatible with Tigray's historical identity and current struggle for self-determination. Self-Determination: Earned, learned, and craved Let us consider the words of Ms. Atsede Gebremedhin (a member of Tigray's 'Shig Weyane' (Revolutionary Torch) in the 1980s. She emphasized her message in Tigrigna, essentially conveying that although her generation envisioned Tigray's future within a federal framework, Ethiopian unity must never be traded for subjugation. When the choice is between self-determination and slavery, the pursuit of independence becomes unavoidable. Her words underscore a timeless principle: no political arrangement is worth sacrificing a people's freedom, dignity, and right to determine their own future. She further detailed her position, which can be, excerpted from the full speech, distilled into the following terms: "...regarding separation [from Ethiopia], we choose separation [independence]. Father Kidanu has been saying, 'We have separation as a second option.' We are putting it as an option, but if a progressive government is promulgated in Ethiopia, it [separation] will not be put as an option. It should not be taken that way. Only if a reactionary and slave system is to come to Ethiopia, we will have to separate ourselves to escape the slavery [oppression]. Therefore, separation is from the slavery and not from working-class people of Ethiopia." More than four decades later, Tigray has endured not only prolonged instability but also the devastating crime of genocide. Its longstanding adversaries, having regrouped after their defeat, returned with renewed force to inflict another wave of devastation marked by persecution, torture, genocide, and betrayal. These experiences have brought the question of self-determination back to the forefront of political consciousness. The aspiration for independence has increasingly gained prominence, finding expression through diverse political platforms, organized movements, public discourse, and cultural expression. Music, in particular, has become an important vehicle for expressing Tigrayan identity, historical consciousness, and national aspirations. Songs such as ዓዲ ኣላትኒ (I Have a Country), ሃ ገር እየ ዝደሊ (What I Want Is Independence), ትግራዋነት (The Essence of Being Tigrayan), ትግራይ ዓደይ (Tigray, My Nation), ትግራይ ኵሕሎ (Beautiful Tigray), ት ግራይ ምልባማ (Tigray, the Land of Wisdom), and many others reflect the growing significance of national identity, belonging, and aspirations for a sovereign future. This aspiration is neither new nor detached from history. It is rooted in generations of struggle and shaped by the historical experience of imperial nation-building and its devastating consequences for Tigray. It has been earned through sacrifice, strengthened by historical experience, and sustained by an enduring desire for freedom and a secured future. Yet, alongside this growing sense of national purpose, one fundamental question remains: How can this aspiration be translated into a viable, sustainable, and peaceful political future for Tigray? One step into a cruel destiny For the Prosperity government, war has served--and continues to serve--as an instrument for breaking the will, resistance, and collective determination of the people of Tigray. When the regime deploys starvation, foreign military forces, political coercion, and the co-optation of local elites to subdue an entire population, the struggle for self-determination ceases to be merely a political preference. It becomes an indispensable safeguard against subjugation and the permanent erosion of a people's freedom. A sober assessment of post-Pretoria reveals a deeply unsettling reality: Tigray appears to be entering the opening phase of a cruel political destiny--subjugation under the rule of the Prosperity government. As Tigray remains unliberated and increasingly subjected to the authority of the central regime, Ethiopia's overriding objective appears to be the dismantling of the political and institutional foundations that sustain Tigray's resistance and struggle for self-determination. Under the guise of pacification and political normalization, the federal government, helped by some Tigrayans who made their peace with the prime minister, appears to be pursuing a strategy of neutralizing resistance through the co-optation of Tigray's political and military elites. By offering administrative appointments, financial and material inducements, and assurances of personal survival, it seeks to hollow out the liberation struggle from within. Former defenders of Tigray's political aspirations risk becoming instruments and mouthpieces of the very central authority they once opposed. This political realignment risks a deeper ideological capitulation. A collective consciousness once anchored in freedom, dignity, and self-determination is gradually giving way to enforced subjugation and political assimilation. As former defenders align themselves with the very authority they once opposed, the moral and political foundations of the struggle erode, undermining its unifying force and leaving society increasingly disarmed--both politically and psychologically--and pressured to surrender long-term freedom for the precarious promise of immediate stability and survival. For those aligned with Abiy Ahmed's government, life under external control appears increasingly acceptable and normal. For those who continue to resist, however, subjugation remains unacceptable at any cost. Meanwhile, the central regime and its local partners increasingly portray the historical struggle led by the TPLF as outdated, destructive, or an obstacle to "peace and development." As these narratives take hold, submission risks being recast as political pragmatism, while historical memory and collective political consciousness are distorted or erased. Future generations may consequently be led to view the sacrifices of their predecessors and the TPLF's struggle not as acts of resistance and defense of the right to self-rule but as misguided and costly mistakes. Coercive assimilation, state-led social engineering What is presented as integration may, under occupation and political subordination, become a state-engineered project of assimilation. By extending central government institutions and security structures into Tigray's social and political life, the state could displace local authority, dismantle sovereign institutions, and erode the foundations of self-governance. Prolonged military occupation could thus serve not merely to administer territory but to impose a far-reaching political and social transformation. This process could entail the imposition of political, cultural, and administrative arrangements through military coercion, legislative control, divide-and-rule tactics, and the systematic suppression of local autonomy. Rather than recognize Tigray's distinct historical experience and political aspirations, the central state could seek to remake its institutions and public life in its own image and in accordance with its political priorities. The danger extends beyond institutional control to demographic and territorial engineering. In the aftermath of mass atrocities, such developments raise grave concerns about whether political domination could evolve into a broader project of demographic transformation, threatening the long-term continuity of the Tigray people. As this trajectory becomes entrenched, many Tigrayans--particularly those unwilling to abandon the pursuit of self-determination--may come to see leaving their homeland as the only remaining means of resisting subjugation. Those who remain, meanwhile, could find themselves trapped in a deeply fractured society, divided between accommodation and resistance, privilege and deprivation, and outward compliance and inward resentment. Tigray risks becoming a society of happy slaves and unhappy slaves--one in which subjugation is normalized for some and silently endured by others. This division between those aligned with the central government and those resisting subjugation could harden into an entrenched system of divide and rule. By cultivating competing loyalties and interests within Tigrayan society, the regime could fracture collective solidarity, weaken organized resistance, and obstruct a unified political response. The result could be an "enemy within" syndrome, in which internal suspicion becomes a major obstacle to future unity. Mutual distrust could gradually replace the quiet solidarity, shared understanding, and knowing glances through which Tigrayans sustained one another during the darkest years of siege and blockade. A society once united by shared suffering and resistance could become consumed by suspicion over who has accommodated the system, who has resisted it, and who can still be trusted. Indefinite social discord The existing horizontal divisions within Tigrayan elites--expressed through political realignments, competing strategic visions, and conflicting interpretations of the postwar order--risk hardening into a prolonged and intergenerational rupture. If centralizing and assimilationist policies become entrenched, Tigray could face not only a political struggle over its future but also an internal war over its history, identity, and collective memory. Self-determination must once again become the organizing principle of Tigray's political future." One generation may grow increasingly exposed to central government-sponsored narratives, while another remains committed to preserving Tigray's historical struggle for self-rule rights, convictions, and aspirations. Such a rupture would not remain confined to political organizations or public institutions. It could penetrate the most intimate structures of the society. The long-term damage would extend far beyond political disagreement, undermining the social trust upon which collective life depends. The collapse of social contract of sacrifice Perhaps one of the most devastating long-term consequences of an unaddressed political defeat and perceived internal betrayal would be the destruction of society's capacity for collective mobilization. When the social contract of sacrifice is broken, a profound cynicism may take hold toward political leadership, military institutions, and the very causes for which ordinary people were once prepared to make extraordinary sacrifices. For a population to endure the horrors of war, there must be a fundamental, often unspoken covenant among the people, their fighters, their leadership, and the cause they serve. That covenant rests on a shared understanding: sacrifice must have meaning; those who fall must be remembered and honored; the suffering of the population must not be exploited; and leaders must not trade away the collective cause for their personal security or political survival. When this covenant is violated, the consequences can endure for generations. The public may lose confidence in those who call for sacrifice, and future appeals for mobilization may be met with profound skepticism. People may no longer regard military mobilization as an honorable defense of their homeland and collective aspirations but as a political instrument through which ordinary citizens bear the ultimate costs while political and military elites negotiate their own survival and interests. The memory of betrayal can therefore become a powerful deterrent to future collective action. Even when an existential threat emerges, a population that has lost confidence in its leadership may hesitate to mobilize, fearing that its sacrifices will once again be squandered or betrayed. ethiopia.content: Eritrea: U.S. Lawmaker Proposes Trade Incentives to Push Ethiopia, Eritrea Off Conflict Cliff, Toward Peace - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Eritrea: U.S. Lawmaker Proposes Trade Incentives to Push Ethiopia, Eritrea Off Conflict Cliff, Toward Peace Ayin Network TPLF fighters (file photo). 20 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — US Republican Representative Jim Baird has proposed two pieces of legislation seeking to link expanded trade and economic cooperation with Ethiopia and Eritrea to progress toward lasting peace, as tensions between the neighboring countries continue to raise fears of a renewed interstate conflict. The proposed Ethiopia SPARK Act and Eritrea PILLAR Act would use US agricultural exports, farm equipment, technical expertise and cooperation in critical minerals development as economic incentives for both countries to pursue peace, according to a report by The Hill published on November 19. The legislation, shared exclusively in draft form with The Hill , also seeks to strengthen US economic influence in the Horn of Africa and reduce China's foothold in the region. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Under the proposed measures, Ethiopia and Eritrea would be offered opportunities for formal trade negotiations and expanded access to US agricultural products, including corn, soybeans, soybean meal and livestock feed, as well as farm machinery, agricultural research and technical assistance, contingent on steps toward establishing lasting peace. The proposals also envisage US assistance in developing the region's mineral resources, including gold, silver, copper, zinc, iron ore, potash, cement, limestone, natural gas and oil, alongside cooperation on port infrastructure. Washington could offer reduced tariffs and improved trade terms as additional incentives. Baird, a Republican from Indiana and member of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on Africa, described the initiative as an opportunity to build economic partnerships with African countries while limiting the influence of US adversaries. "African nations are primed for partnership," Baird said in a statement to The Hill . "The continent is rich in natural resources and home to a young, growing population eager for greater economic opportunity. In Indiana and across America's heartland, we have the agricultural expertise and technological know-how to help unlock that potential and build lasting economic partnerships." "East Africa has tremendous potential, with the benefit of limited influence from America's adversaries, like China," he added. Baird said the proposed economic cooperation could provide a foundation for regional stability and prosperity, arguing that African countries pursuing peaceful cooperation and economic growth would find a willing partner in the United States. The initiative comes amid a sharp deterioration in relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea, with competing claims over sovereign Red Sea access, mutual accusations of interference and reported military buildups along their shared border heightening fears of a wider confrontation. The deteriorating diplomatic relations between the two countries broke down on October 1, following Ethiopia's closure of its embassy in Asmara and the expulsion of Eritrean diplomats, a move reciprocated by Eritrea . Both governments have subsequently exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, while reports of troop movements, drone strikes and artillery activity around the disputed border town of Badme have intensified concerns about a possible military escalation. In a statement issued Thursday, Nov. 19, GCC Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi expressed support for the UAE amid escalating diplomatic tensions between Mogadishu and Abu Dhabi. advertisements Albudaiwi criticized statements by officials of Somalia's federal government, accusing them of spreading allegations that undermine the UAE's regional and international role. The GCC statement described the remarks as irresponsible and denounced what it called malicious media campaigns directed against one of its member states. The secretary-general defended the UAE's diplomatic activities, saying the country had made significant contributions to regional security, stability and international dialogue. “The UAE’s recent hosting of Russian-Ukrainian talks demonstrates its commitment to regional and international peace and security. These unacceptable allegations seek to undermine our efforts to promote dialogue and cooperation,” he said. Albudaiwi said the allegations against the UAE risked undermining its efforts to promote regional and international cooperation. He emphasized that GCC member states remained committed to advancing peace, stability and prosperity and would reject campaigns intended to damage the reputation of any member state. “The GCC states remain steadfast in their approach to consolidating security, stability, and prosperity, and categorically reject any media campaigns aimed at offending any of their member states. Such campaigns will not affect the continuation of their role in supporting peace and security across the region and the world,” the statement added. The statement comes amid a sharp deterioration in diplomatic relations between Somalia and the UAE following accusations by President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud that Abu Dhabi has interfered in Somalia's domestic political and security affairs. In a televised address Tuesday, Hassan Sheikh accused the UAE of providing political, financial and security support to regional administrations and armed groups operating outside the federal government's control. He also criticized Emirati agreements involving the ports of Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo, arguing that such arrangements undermine Somalia's sovereignty and should be negotiated through Mogadishu. On Thursday, Somalia's Cabinet ordered the UAE ambassador to leave the country within 72 hours and recalled its ambassador from Abu Dhabi for consultations. The Somali government said the measures were intended to protect its sovereignty, territorial integrity and national unity. The UAE Foreign Ministry responded by condemning what it described as the Somali government's hostile approach, accusing Mogadishu of allowing internal political disputes to damage bilateral relations. Abu Dhabi also said it had closed its embassy in Mogadishu and withdrawn its diplomatic personnel in January 2026, following earlier disagreements over Somalia's cancellation of bilateral agreements. The GCC's latest statement adds a regional dimension to the dispute, with the six-member Gulf bloc publicly defending the UAE against Somalia's accusations. The GCC comprises the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman. The council did not announce any diplomatic or economic measures against Somalia, limiting its response to a public condemnation of the Somali government's statements and expressions of support for the UAE. somalia.content: Somalia, EU host security talks in Brussels ahead of AUSSOM mandate decision - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia, EU host security talks in Brussels ahead of AUSSOM mandate decision Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Saturday November 21, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somalia and the European Union have jointly hosted a high-level security meeting in Brussels, bringing together representatives from 50 countries and international organizations to discuss Somalia's plan to assume full responsibility for national security as the future of the African Union peacekeeping mission comes under review. The meeting, held Thursday, Nov. 19, focused on Somalia's security transition roadmap, the future of international military assistance and efforts to strengthen the country's security institutions ahead of a United Nations Security Council decision on the mandate of the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) in December. advertisements According to Somalia's Ministry of Defence, the gathering provided an opportunity for the federal government to present its vision for taking full responsibility for national security while coordinating future support from international partners. Somali Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi addressed the opening session, outlining the country's security situation, progress in the transition process and the government's plans to assume greater security responsibilities. Fiqi emphasized the importance of continued international assistance to ensure an orderly transition that reflects Somalia's security priorities and operational needs. Jihan Abdullahi Hassan, senior adviser to President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud on defense affairs, presented Somalia's security transition strategy, outlining the government's proposed framework for transferring responsibilities from international forces to Somali institutions. The meeting was co-chaired by Abdihakim Mohamed Yusuf, chief of staff to the Somali president, and Olof Skoog, deputy secretary-general for political affairs at the European External Action Service. Other participants included Annette Weber, the EU special representative for the Horn of Africa; El Hadji Ibrahima Diene, the African Union special representative for Somalia and head of AUSSOM; and Graham Maitland, the United Nations director for East Africa in the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs. Representatives from AUSSOM troop-contributing countries, including Djibouti, Ethiopia, Kenya and Uganda, attended the discussions alongside officials from the United States, United Kingdom, Türkiye, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait and EU member states. According to the European Union, participants discussed future international engagement in Somalia's security framework and the importance of maintaining close coordination during the transition. They agreed to continue technical and political consultations to develop a common understanding of the next steps. The EU also emphasized that a sustainable security framework would require broader political agreement among Somali stakeholders, highlighting the importance of an inclusive political settlement. The discussions come as AUSSOM faces uncertainty over its future financing and operations. The mission's current United Nations authorization expires Dec. 31, 2026, and the Security Council is expected to consider its renewal next month. Funding shortages have raised concerns about the ability of African Union forces to maintain operations and continue supporting Somali troops fighting al-Shabab. Some troop-contributing countries have also announced plans to reduce or withdraw their military presence, increasing pressure on Somalia to strengthen its armed forces and assume responsibility for areas previously secured by international peacekeepers. AUSSOM, which replaced the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia in January 2025, supports Somali security forces in operations against al-Shabab and in protecting strategic locations. Despite years of military operations, al-Shabab continues to carry out attacks and maintain a presence in parts of southern and central Somalia. The European Union reaffirmed its commitment to supporting Somalia's peace, stability and security, including a transition led and managed by Somali institutions. Officials attending the Brussels meeting welcomed Somalia's proposed security transition framework and called for closer cooperation to ensure that progress is sustained. However, no final agreement on future security arrangements or new financial commitments was announced. Facebook Instagram X VKontakte Youtube Somali Guardian News Somalia Africa World Featured Editor Picks Editorials Home News Somalia Somalia opposition rejects another request for talks from president Hassan Sheikh Mohamud Somalia opposition rejects another request for talks from president Hassan Sheikh Mohamud November 21, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somalia’s opposition leaders have unanimously rejected any talks with President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud after he telephoned former Prime Minister Abdi Farah Shirdon and asked him to host the meeting at his home. The president promised major concessions and said Somalia’s future and upcoming elections would be settled through broad-based consensus. Shirdon relayed the offer. Opposition leaders met at length on Thursday night, debated the proposal, and reconvened on Friday. In that second session they rejected both the meeting and any further engagement with Mohamud. The refusal follows earlier talks that collapsed because the president made no meaningful concessions and continued to insist on a one-person, one-vote election conducted on terms he favors—an arrangement widely viewed as intended to secure him a third term. Opposition leaders demand that Mohamud first abandon this model and accept that both the type of election and the manner in which it is held must be decided through a consensus process involving all political stakeholders. The president has stated that no decision will be placed “in the middle,” conveying that only the government will determine the election model and the country’s political direction, while others may merely offer advice that may or may not be considered. Further opposition conditions include international mediation, binding guarantees that the president will negotiate in good faith, reversal of the election model and the constitutional changes he has introduced, and security assurances for the presidents of Puntland and other regional states as well as other attending leaders. Mohamud’s approach to Shirdon, regarded as one of the less hardline opposition figures, comes under intensifying international pressure. Western and East African partners had already urged dialogue; Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Egypt have now joined calls for an electoral agreement to avert an irreversible crisis. Opposition leaders view the latest offer as a tactical maneuver designed to occupy, divide, and co-opt members of their coalition—the same method previously used to draw former parliamentary speaker Sharif Hassan Sheikh Adan, former Prime Minister Omar Abdirashid, and Dahir Mohamud Gelle into supporting the president’s election model after they attended earlier talks. A previous opposition-wide conference scheduled for the 14th of this month also failed to take place after the opposition insisted its core demands be met in advance and the president refused. The standoff unfolds amid a severe political, constitutional, and security crisis. Somalia’s Constitutional Court recently ruled that Mohamud is unlawfully in office, declared his term extension null and void, ordered elections within 90 days, and required a political agreement within 30 days. A Government of Political Theatre, Misleading Statements, and Weak Leadership Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Abdiaziz Hassan Giyaajo Amalo Friday November 20, 2026\ Somalia deserves a Prime Minister who understands the responsibilities of his office, exercises independent leadership, and communicates honestly with the Somali people. Unfortunately, the current political environment raises serious questions about the effectiveness, authority, and credibility of the Prime Minister. His public statements concerning the United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) illustrate the growing problem of political communication in Mogadishu: taking credit for international decisions, confusing separate United Nations mandates, and presenting developments beyond the government’s control as achievements of the federal administration. The Prime Minister should explain precisely what his government has accomplished regarding UNSOS. Did the Federal Government formally cancel the mission, or did an existing United Nations mandate reach its scheduled expiration date? These are fundamentally different matters, and the Somali public deserves an honest explanation. UNSOS Is Not the Same as UNTMIS There is an important distinction that the Prime Minister should understand before making public declarations. The United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) officially concluded its operations on October 31, 2026, following a two-year transition requested by the Somali government. UNSOS, however, is a separate United Nations operation responsible for providing essential logistical support to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) and participating Somali security forces. According to the United Nations, UNSOS’s existing authorization for 2026 remains in place, with the current AUSSOM authorization scheduled to expire on December 31, 2026. Furthermore, discussions about the future of UNSOS involve international funding decisions, particularly the position of the United States, one of its major financial supporters. Therefore, claiming that the Somali government independently cancelled UNSOS would require documentary evidence and clarification from the United Nations Security Council. An Empty Suit at the Top of Government The deeper problem is not simply one statement about the United Nations. It is the apparent absence of strong, independent executive leadership. A Prime Minister should not function as a ceremonial spokesperson whose principal responsibility is to defend presidential decisions or announce political victories that have not been achieved. Somalia needs a Prime Minister who can challenge bad policies, demand accountability, coordinate national institutions, and represent the interests of the entire country. A government cannot build public confidence through political publicity while the country continues to experience insecurity, constitutional disagreements, institutional weaknesses, and economic hardship. The Prime Minister must demonstrate that his office has genuine authority and is not merely an extension of Villa Somalia. Somalia Needs Leadership, Not Political Public Relations At a time when Somalia faces serious political and security challenges, the country cannot afford leadership built around exaggerated announcements and misleading political narratives. The Prime Minister should answer several important questions: 1. Did the Federal Government officially request the cancellation of UNSOS? 2. Is there a formal United Nations Security Council decision terminating UNSOS? 3. Why is the government presenting the conclusion of UNTMIS as though it were the cancellation of UNSOS? 4. What alternative logistical arrangements will support AUSSOM and Somali security forces if international assistance is reduced? 5. What independent authority does the Prime Minister exercise in making national policy? These are legitimate questions of public accountability, not personal attacks. Conclusion: Somalia Deserves a Real Prime Minister Somalia does not need an empty suit occupying the office of Prime Minister. It needs a serious statesman capable of exercising constitutional authority, defending national interests, and telling the Somali people the truth. Leadership is not measured by press conferences, political slogans, or the ability to take credit for decisions made by international institutions. It is measured by results, integrity, accountability, and the ability to govern. If the Prime Minister cannot distinguish between the expiration of one United Nations mission and the continuing mandate of another, the public has every reason to demand a clearer explanation. Somalia needs leadership, not political theatre. The office of Prime Minister must represent national responsibility, not merely serve as a political decoration inside Villa Somalia. Important factual distinction: UNTMIS closed on October 31, 2026. UNSOS is separate, and its current 2026 authorization has not yet expired as of November 19, 2026. The distinction is documented by the United Nations UNSOS mandate⁠. football.title: أزمة الدوري السوداني.. المريخ يتسلم الحيثيات ويستعد لـ"كاس" - www.winwin.com
football.summary: تسلم نادي المريخ السوداني، في 20 نوفمبر 2026، الحيثيات التي استندت إليها لجنة الاستئنافات باتحاد كرة القدم السوداني في قرارها بإعادة لقب الدوري الممتاز لنادي الهلال، بعد أن كان قد مُنح سابقًا للمريخ. وقد أثار هذا القرار ردود أفعال واسعة، حيث كانت اللجنة قد قبلت في البداية طعن المريخ. الآن، يستعد المريخ لتقديم مذكرة إلى محكمة التحكيم الرياضية "كاس" بعد تقييم الحيثيات، في خطوة تهدف لاستعادة اللقب. يأتي ذلك في إطار الضغط المستمر من إدارة النادي على اتحاد كرة القدم، مستندة إلى تجربة سابقة في 2017 حيث تم منح المريخ اللقب عبر قرار قضائي. الصراع القانوني بين المريخ والهلال يتصاعد، خاصة بعد الطعن في قانونية مشاركة بعض لاعبي الهلال في مباراة الديربي.

football.summary: مدرب الهلال السوداني، الألماني جوزيف زينباور، يستعد لمواجهة فريق الشرطة الرواندي في مباراة حاسمة ضمن الجولة الثامنة من الدوري الرواندي، المقررة يوم 20 نوفمبر. الهلال يسعى لتحقيق الفوز لتعزيز موقعه في جدول الترتيب، حيث يملك ثلاث مباريات مؤجلة. يواجه زينباور ثلاثة تحديات رئيسية، تشمل غيابات مؤثرة بسبب إرهاق اللاعبين الذين شاركوا مع المنتخب في تصفيات كأس الأمم الأفريقية، مما قد يؤثر على أداء الفريق. كما أن المدرب غاب عن تدريبات الفريق لمدة 11 يومًا خلال فترة التوقف الدولي، مما زاد من صعوبة التحضير للمباراة. الهلال يعاني من تراجع في مستوى لاعبيه الأساسيين، ويعمل زينباور على إعادة الروح المعنوية للفريق بعد الهزائم الأخيرة. يهدف الهلال إلى تحقيق نتائج إيجابية في الدوري الرواندي ودوري أبطال أفريقيا، حيث يسعى لتحقيق إنجازات جديدة.

football.summary: تستعد الجماهير السودانية لانطلاق النسخة 31 من الدوري السوداني الممتاز لموسم 2026-2027، المقرر أن يبدأ يوم الأربعاء 25 نوفمبر بمباراة تجمع بين الهلال حامل اللقب والأهلي مروي. يواجه اتحاد كرة القدم المحلي تحديات كبيرة، بما في ذلك عدم جاهزية الملاعب وصعوبات لوجستية نتيجة الأوضاع الأمنية المتدهورة. تضررت البنية التحتية الرياضية بشكل كبير بسبب الحرب التي اندلعت في أبريل 2023، مما أدى إلى تأجيل المنافسة في البداية. رغم هذه الظروف، تسعى بعض الاتحادات الولائية لتأهيل الملاعب، لكن معظمها لا يزال غير جاهز. بالإضافة إلى ذلك، تعاني الأندية من صعوبات اقتصادية، مما أثر على استعداداتها. تم تغيير نظام المنافسة ليشمل مرحلتين، حيث تتأهل 8 أندية للمرحلة النهائية المعروفة بـ"دوري النخبة". يأمل الجميع في نجاح الموسم رغم التحديات الراهنة.
